States of Matter.intro: The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids and gases in terms of how particles are arranged and how they move.
States of Matter.mnemonic: "Solid Stays, Liquid Loves to flow, Gas Goes everywhere" — remember the three states by what particles DO.

sections.title: The Three States
sections.text: All matter exists as solid, liquid or gas. The state depends on how strongly particles are attracted to each other and how much energy they have.
points: Solid — particles close together in regular pattern; vibrate about fixed positions; cannot flow; not compressible
Liquid — particles close together but random arrangement; move freely past each other; can flow; not compressible
Gas — particles far apart; random arrangement; move quickly in all directions; can flow; easily compressed
Shape and volume — solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take shape of container; gases fill any container
Compressibility — only gases are compressible because there is large empty space between particles

sections.title: Internal Energy
sections.text: The internal energy of a substance is the total kinetic and potential energy of all its particles. Heating increases internal energy.
points: Internal energy — total kinetic + potential energy of all particles in the substance
Heating increases internal energy — particles move faster (kinetic energy increases)
Temperature — a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles; higher temp = faster particles
Heat vs temperature — heat is energy transferred; temperature measures average KE; they are NOT the same
Potential energy — related to the separation of particles and intermolecular forces between them

sections.title: Particle Arrangement and Forces
sections.text: Intermolecular forces hold particles together. The balance between forces and kinetic energy determines the state of a substance.
points: Intermolecular forces — attractive forces between particles; strongest in solids, weakest in gases
Regular lattice (solid) — particles locked into repeating 3D pattern with strong forces between them
Random arrangement (liquid/gas) — particles have enough energy to overcome the regular lattice
Pressure from gases — gas particles collide with container walls, exerting force per unit area
Brownian motion — random movement of particles in a fluid caused by collisions with surrounding molecules

keyTerms.def: A model that explains properties of matter using the movement and arrangement of particles
Total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a substance
A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance
Attractive force between particles — strongest in solids, weakest in gases
The ability to be squashed into a smaller volume — only gases are compressible
Random motion of particles in a fluid caused by collisions with surrounding molecules

examTips: Temperature measures average kinetic energy — higher temperature = particles move faster. Never say particles in solids are stationary — they vibrate.
Gases are compressible; solids and liquids are not — particles in gases are far apart with lots of empty space between them.
AQA often asks you to 'use the particle model to explain' a property — always link particle arrangement/movement to the macroscopic property being asked about.
commonMistakes: Saying all particles in a solid are stationary — they vibrate around fixed positions; they just don't move from place to place.
Confusing temperature (average KE per particle) with heat/internal energy (total energy of all particles).
Saying liquids are compressible — liquids cannot be compressed because particles are already touching each other.
clozePassages: Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. In a solid, particles are closely packed in regular arrangements and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, particles are close together but can move around each other. In a gas, particles are far apart and move rapidly in random directions. The properties of each state — shape, volume, compressibility — follow from the arrangement and movement of particles.

The differences between states of matter can be explained by the particle model. Solids have fixed shapes and cannot be compressed because particles are close together. Liquids take the shape of their container but cannot be compressed. Gases expand to fill their container and can be compressed because particles are widely spaced. The particle model successfully explains macroscopic properties in terms of microscopic particle behaviour.

In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions but the average positions form a regular lattice. In a liquid, intermolecular forces are weaker, allowing particles to slide past each other — liquids can flow. In a gas, particles have sufficient kinetic energy to overcome all intermolecular forces and move independently. The particle model also explains why gases exert pressure — particles constantly collide with container walls, exerting a force.

Changes of State.intro: When substances are heated or cooled they can change state. These changes involve energy transfers and are physical, not chemical, changes.
Changes of State.mnemonic: "Melting Boils Every Condensed Freezing Substance" — Melting, Boiling, Evaporating, Condensing, Freezing, Sublimating. Or remember: heating ABSORBS energy (endothermic); cooling RELEASES energy (exothermic).

sections.title: Changes of State
sections.text: Matter can change between states when energy is added or removed. These are physical changes — the substance itself remains the same.
points: Melting — solid → liquid (absorb energy); occurs at the melting point
Boiling/evaporating — liquid → gas (absorb energy); boiling at fixed point, evaporation at any temperature
Condensing — gas → liquid (release energy); releases latent heat of vaporisation
Freezing — liquid → solid (release energy); releases latent heat of fusion
Sublimation — solid → gas directly (e.g. dry ice, iodine)

sections.title: Latent Heat
sections.text: Latent heat is the energy transferred during a change of state without a temperature change. It is used to break or form intermolecular bonds.

callout.label: Why Temperature Stays Constant
callout.text: During a change of state, temperature stays constant even though energy is being supplied. The energy is used to break intermolecular bonds (latent heat), not to increase KE of particles.

points: Specific latent heat of fusion (L_f) — energy to melt/freeze 1 kg at constant temperature; unit: J/kg
Specific latent heat of vaporisation (L_v) — energy to boil/condense 1 kg; larger than L_f
Formula: Q = mL — energy (J) = mass (kg) × specific latent heat (J/kg)
Worked example — melting 2 kg of ice (L_f = 334 000 J/kg): Q = 2 × 334 000 = 668 000 J
Why L_v > L_f — vaporisation requires complete separation of particles; fusion only partially disrupts structure

sections.title: Heating Curves
sections.text: A heating curve shows how temperature changes as energy is added. Flat sections show where latent heat is being absorbed during a change of state.
points: Rising sections — temperature increases as kinetic energy of particles increases (Q = mcΔT)
Flat sections — temperature constant during melting or boiling; energy breaks intermolecular bonds
Melting point — first flat section; solid converting to liquid
Boiling point — second flat section; liquid converting to gas
Steepness — slope of rising section depends on specific heat capacity (less steep = higher SHC)

keyTerms.def: Energy absorbed or released during a change of state — no temperature change
Energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing temperature (J/kg)
Liquid → gas at any temperature (from the surface only)
Liquid → gas throughout the liquid at a fixed boiling point
Direct change from solid to gas without passing through liquid state
Graph of temperature vs energy supplied; flat sections show changes of state

examTips: During a change of state, temperature is CONSTANT — energy goes into breaking bonds, not heating particles. This is a very common AQA 'explain' question.
Q = mL for latent heat calculations; Q = mcΔT for temperature change calculations. Know which to use and when.
Latent heat of vaporisation > latent heat of fusion for the same substance — vaporisation requires complete separation of particles.
commonMistakes: Saying temperature rises during melting — it stays constant at the melting point until all the solid has melted.
Confusing evaporation (any temperature, surface only) with boiling (specific boiling point, throughout the liquid).
Forgetting units: specific latent heat is in J/kg, NOT J/kg°C — there is no temperature change involved.
clozePassages: Changes of state are physical changes — the chemical composition does not change. Melting (solid to liquid) and boiling (liquid to gas) both require energy input to overcome the forces between particles. Condensation (gas to liquid) and freezing (liquid to solid) release energy as forces between particles form. During a change of state, temperature remains constant even though energy is being supplied or released.

The energy needed to change state without changing temperature is called latent heat. The specific latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to melt 1 kg of a substance. The specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to vaporise 1 kg. These values are much larger than the specific heat capacity values because energy is needed to break intermolecular bonds rather than just increase particle speed.

A heating curve shows how temperature changes as energy is supplied to a substance. Temperature rises steadily as energy increases the kinetic energy of particles. During a change of state (melting or boiling), temperature stays constant — energy is used to break bonds between particles, not to increase temperature. The flat sections on a heating curve show the melting point and boiling point of the substance.

Density.intro: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance. It explains why some materials float and others sink.
Density.mnemonic: "Ducks Must Visit ponds" — Density = Mass ÷ Volume. Or think of ρ (rho) as 'rho = m over V'.

sections.title: Density Formula
sections.text: Density links mass and volume. A substance is denser if more mass is packed into the same volume.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: ρ = m/V (density = mass ÷ volume). Units: kg/m³ or g/cm³. Rearranged: m = ρV and V = m/ρ.

points: ρ = m/V — density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) ÷ volume (m³)
Unit conversion — 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³; be careful in calculations
Worked example — mass = 500 g = 0.5 kg; volume = 250 cm³ = 0.00025 m³; ρ = 0.5/0.00025 = 2000 kg/m³
Denser states — solids generally denser than liquids; liquids denser than gases (particles more closely packed)
Ice anomaly — ice is less dense than liquid water (unusual) — particles in ice lattice are more spread out

sections.title: Measuring Density
sections.text: Density can be measured experimentally by finding mass and volume separately, then calculating using ρ = m/V.
points: Regular solid — measure mass with balance; calculate volume from dimensions (l × w × h); ρ = m/V
Irregular solid — measure mass with balance; use displacement can (eureka can) to find volume
Displacement method — volume of water displaced = volume of object; read from measuring cylinder
Liquid — measure mass of empty then filled measuring cylinder; volume read directly from cylinder
Accuracy — use a top-pan balance for mass (to 2 d.p. in grams); repeat volume measurements

sections.title: Floating and Sinking
sections.text: Whether an object floats or sinks depends on how its density compares to the density of the fluid it is placed in.
points: Floats — if object density < fluid density (e.g. wood in water; ρ_wood ≈ 600 kg/m³ < ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³)
Sinks — if object density > fluid density (e.g. iron; ρ_iron ≈ 7900 kg/m³ > ρ_water)
Upthrust — buoyancy force pushing up on a submerged object; equal to weight of fluid displaced
Ships float — even though steel is dense, the hull traps air — average density of ship < water
Layering of fluids — less dense fluids float on denser ones (oil on water)

keyTerms.def: Mass per unit volume of a substance: ρ = m/V; units kg/m³ or g/cm³
Volume of water displaced by a submerged object equals the object's volume
The upward buoyancy force on an object submerged in a fluid
Overflow can used to measure the volume of an irregular solid by water displacement
The amount of space occupied by an object, measured in m³ or cm³
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kg — does not change with location

examTips: ρ = m/V — learn this formula and both rearrangements (m = ρV and V = m/ρ). Units must be consistent: use kg and m³, or g and cm³.
For irregular shapes, use the water displacement method — the volume of water displaced equals the object's volume. AQA may ask you to describe the method step-by-step.
Unit conversion trap: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. If density is given in g/cm³ and mass in kg, convert carefully before calculating.
commonMistakes: Confusing density with mass — a large object isn't necessarily denser than a small one. Density depends on how tightly particles are packed.
Forgetting to convert units — 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Mixing units in calculations gives wrong answers.
Saying denser objects always sink — an object floats if its density is LESS than the fluid, regardless of its mass.
clozePassages: Density is defined as mass per unit volume. The formula is ρ = m/V, where ρ is density, m is mass in kg, and V is volume in m³. Density is measured in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Solids are generally denser than liquids, which are denser than gases, because particles are more closely packed. Ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why it floats — an unusual property that is crucial for aquatic life in cold climates.

The density of a regular solid can be calculated by measuring its mass using a balance and its volume by calculation from its dimensions. The density of an irregular solid can be found using a eureka can or displacement method — the volume of water displaced equals the volume of the object. The density of a liquid can be measured by weighing a known volume using a measuring cylinder.

Materials with different densities will separate when mixed, with denser materials sinking and less dense materials floating. This explains why oil floats on water and why a stone sinks. The density of gases is much lower than solids and liquids because the particles are widely spread. Hot air is less dense than cold air because the particles move faster and spread out more, which is why hot air rises and is used in hot air balloons.

Specific Heat Capacity.intro: Specific heat capacity (SHC) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. It explains why different materials heat up at different rates.
Specific Heat Capacity.mnemonic: "Every Mug Contains Delta-Temperature" — E = mcΔT. The 'm' is mass, 'c' is SHC, and ΔT is the temperature change.

🖼️

sections.title: The Formula
sections.text: The specific heat capacity equation links the energy transferred to the mass, material, and temperature change.

callout.label: Formula
callout.text: Q = mcΔT — Energy (J) = mass (kg) × SHC (J/kg°C) × temperature change (°C). Rearranged: c = Q/(mΔT) and ΔT = Q/(mc).

points: Q = mcΔT — Q in joules, m in kg, c in J/kg°C, ΔT in °C or K
ΔT = T_final − T_initial — always use the CHANGE in temperature, not the final temperature
Worked example — heat 2 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg°C) by 10°C: Q = 2 × 4200 × 10 = 84 000 J
High SHC — material needs more energy to heat up; heats slowly but also cools slowly
Water's SHC — 4200 J/kg°C; very high compared to metals (e.g. copper ≈ 385 J/kg°C)

sections.title: Practical: Finding SHC
sections.text: The SHC of a material can be measured experimentally using an electric heater and thermometer.
points: Method — heat known mass with immersion heater; record energy from E = P × t (power × time)
Calculate SHC — c = Q ÷ (m × ΔT); compare to accepted value
Source of error — energy lost to surroundings means measured c is HIGHER than true value
Improving accuracy — insulate the block; stir liquid; use a lid; place thermometer in block not in heater hole
Joulemeter — measures energy directly and more accurately than P × t

sections.title: Applications
sections.text: High specific heat capacity has many practical applications in storing and transferring thermal energy.
points: Water as coolant — high SHC means it absorbs large amounts of energy without getting too hot; used in car engines and nuclear reactors
Sea moderates climate — heats and cools slowly; coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland
Central heating — water carries energy from boiler to radiators efficiently due to high SHC
Sweating — body uses water's high SHC to regulate temperature; evaporation removes thermal energy
Storage heaters — use materials with high SHC (e.g. clay bricks) to store heat overnight and release slowly

keyTerms.def: Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C; unit: J/kg°C
Total energy needed to raise the temperature of an object by 1°C (mass × SHC)
The difference between final and initial temperature: ΔT = T_final − T_initial
Electrical heating element placed directly in a material to supply a known amount of energy
Device that measures electrical energy transferred directly in joules
Material used to reduce unwanted energy transfer to surroundings in SHC experiments

examTips: Water has a very high SHC (4200 J/kg°C) — AQA commonly asks you to explain why water is used as a coolant or why coastal areas have mild climates. The answer is always high SHC.
In SHC practicals, the measured value will be HIGHER than the true value because energy is lost to surroundings, not all going into the material.
Always use ΔT (temperature change) in Q = mcΔT — never substitute the final temperature alone. If water starts at 20°C and reaches 80°C, ΔT = 60°C.
commonMistakes: Using the final temperature instead of ΔT (change in temperature) in calculations — this gives a wildly wrong answer.
Forgetting to convert mass to kg if given in grams — 500 g = 0.5 kg.
Saying a material with a high SHC heats up quickly — it is the OPPOSITE: high SHC means more energy is needed, so it heats up more slowly.
clozePassages: The specific heat capacity (SHC) of a material is the energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the material by 1°C. It is measured in J/kg°C. The equation used is: E = mc∆T, where E is energy in joules, m is mass in kg, c is the specific heat capacity, and ∆T is the temperature change. Different materials have different specific heat capacities — water has a very high value of 4200 J/kg°C.

The high specific heat capacity of water has important consequences. Water is used as a coolant in car engines and nuclear reactors because it can absorb large amounts of energy before its temperature rises significantly. The sea moderates coastal climates because it heats up and cools down more slowly than land. The human body uses water to regulate temperature through sweating — evaporation of sweat removes large amounts of thermal energy from the body.

To measure specific heat capacity experimentally, an electric heater is used to supply a known amount of energy to a sample of known mass. The temperature change is recorded using a thermometer. The specific heat capacity is calculated from c = E/(m∆T). To minimise errors, the sample should be insulated to reduce heat loss to the surroundings. The actual value will be slightly higher than the true value due to energy losses.

Gas Pressure.intro: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of their container. Temperature, volume and pressure are all related.
Gas Pressure.mnemonic: "Pressured particles Push more when they're Hot or Hemmed in" — Pressure increases when temperature rises (faster particles) or volume decreases (more frequent collisions).

Diagram: Gas Pressure

sections.title: What Causes Gas Pressure?
sections.text: Gas pressure is the result of billions of gas particles constantly colliding with the walls of their container, exerting a force per unit area.
points: Particle collisions — gas particles move randomly and collide with container walls, exerting a tiny force each time
Pressure = force/area — billions of collisions per second create a measurable pressure on the walls
Higher temperature — particles move faster → more frequent and harder collisions → higher pressure
Smaller volume — particles hit walls more often per second → higher pressure
More particles — more particles in same volume = more collisions per second = higher pressure

sections.title: Pressure-Volume Relationship (Boyle's Law)
sections.text: At constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional — compressing a gas increases its pressure.

callout.label: Boyle's Law
callout.text: At constant temperature: pressure × volume = constant. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. Compress gas (↓V) → pressure increases (↑P).

points: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ — use this equation for pressure-volume calculations at constant temperature
Inverse relationship — doubling pressure halves volume; halving pressure doubles volume
Worked example — gas at 100 kPa, 2 L compressed to 1 L: P₂ = 100 × 2 ÷ 1 = 200 kPa
Particle explanation — smaller volume means particles hit walls more frequently → higher pressure
Units — pressure in Pa or kPa; volume in m³ or cm³; keep consistent throughout

sections.title: Temperature and Pressure
sections.text: Increasing temperature at constant volume increases pressure because particles move faster and collide more energetically with the walls.
points: Temperature ∝ pressure — at constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature (Kelvin)
Absolute zero (0 K = −273°C) — theoretical temperature where particles have minimum kinetic energy and pressure → 0
Kelvin conversion — K = °C + 273 (always use Kelvin in gas law calculations)
P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ — pressure-temperature law at constant volume
Worked example — gas at 300 K, 100 kPa heated to 600 K: P₂ = 100 × 600 ÷ 300 = 200 kPa

keyTerms.def: Force per unit area exerted by gas particles colliding with container walls; unit: Pa (pascal)
Theoretical minimum temperature (0 K = −273°C) where particles have minimum kinetic energy
At constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂)
Absolute temperature scale starting at absolute zero; K = °C + 273
SI unit of pressure — 1 Pa = 1 N/m²; atmospheric pressure ≈ 100 000 Pa
A theoretical gas that perfectly obeys the gas laws; real gases deviate at high pressure or very low temperature

examTips: Always explain gas pressure using particle collisions — AQA mark schemes require you to mention both the frequency AND force of collisions. Saying 'more collisions' alone may not gain full marks.
P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ — use this for pressure-volume calculations at constant temperature. Always check units are consistent (both pressures in same unit, both volumes in same unit).
Kelvin = Celsius + 273. ALWAYS convert to Kelvin before using gas law equations involving temperature. Forgetting this is a very common mark-losing error.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert °C to Kelvin for gas law calculations — using Celsius in the formula gives completely wrong answers.
Saying gas pressure is caused by gravity — it is caused by particle collisions with the walls, not gravity.
Ignoring direction of change — if volume decreases, pressure must increase (they are inversely proportional); if temperature increases, pressure increases (directly proportional).
clozePassages: Gas pressure is caused by the constant collisions of gas particles with the walls of their container. The more frequent and energetic the collisions, the higher the pressure. If the volume of a container is reduced at constant temperature, particles collide more frequently with the walls, increasing pressure. This is described by Boyle's Law: for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume = constant (pV = constant).

Increasing the temperature of a gas increases the average kinetic energy of its particles. They move faster and collide with the container walls more frequently and with greater force, increasing pressure. At constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature (in kelvin). Absolute zero (0 K = -273°C) is the temperature at which particles have minimum possible kinetic energy and gas pressure would be zero.

The kelvin scale is used in gas law calculations. The relationship between Celsius and kelvin is: T(K) = T(°C) + 273. Gas pressure, volume, and temperature are related by the equation: pV/T = constant for a fixed mass of gas. This allows scientists to predict how a gas behaves under different conditions. The behaviour of real gases deviates from this ideal model at very high pressures or very low temperatures.
